key_insight: Reasoning in diffusion-based video models emerges primarily along the diffusion denoising steps (the denoising trajectory), not as a sequential Chain-of-Frames across time; intervening in the denoising process disrupts reasoning more than intervening across frames.
problem_solved: Clarifies the mechanism behind surprising reasoning abilities in video diffusion models by disproving the prevailing Chain-of-Frames hypothesis and identifying the true locus of reasoning, enabling better analysis and targeted model design.
method: Design interventions and probes that selectively perturb denoising steps versus frame-wise information to trace where reasoning signals form.
Compare qualitative and quantitative metrics (e.g., task performance, attention/latent activations) under step-wise and frame-wise ablations to test CoF vs denoising hypotheses.
Visualize denoising trajectories and perform controlled experiments (freeze/perturb steps, alter noise schedules) to demonstrate causality of denoising dynamics for reasoning.
impact: Reorients research and engineering efforts toward the denoising process as the key target for interpretability, diagnostics, and architecture improvements in video diffusion models, leading to more effective debugging and design strategies.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: Chain-of-Frames (temporal chain) vs Denoising-Steps (stepwise reasoning) to illustrate contrasting hypotheses

paper_authors: Ruisi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Fanyi Pu, Junxiang Xu, Wanqi Yin
